correctionToCP109.claim: CP-109 describes the failure as a class and names two confirmed instances.
correctionToCP109.measured: Across 567 guard sites in the active chain: 53 blocks never execute. ONE is a high-severity control that was believed in force and was not (DB015-K1, already found and fixed by DB-014). 13 are medium, 38 are low or informational, and the overwhelming majority of those are defensive repairs and post-condition assertions that are CORRECTLY INERT — the block doing nothing is what it was written to do.
correction: The class is real and it is a FAMILY, not two instances: 14 RLS-policy blocks across four migrations and eight tables, plus four `is null then return` guards that skip the rest of their block, plus four `drop policy`-only blocks, plus ten inert post-condition assertions. That is 32 of the 52.

The class is also NARROWER than CP-109's framing implies. CP-109's language — 'not a weaker control, it is an absent one' — is exactly right for DB015-K1 and for the four drop-policy blocks in principle, and wrong for the other 47. A guard on a table the chain never creates is not an absent control; it is a note about a table that does not exist. A conditional column back-fill that never runs is not an absent control; it is a repair for a problem the main DDL already solved. Reporting 52 findings at one severity would be the same class of error as reporting one finding at high: it makes the list unreadable and trains people to ignore it.

The measurement that would have caught the over-reporting is the same shape as the measurement that found the bug: for each block, ask what the block's OWN bytes were trying to do, and ask whether its subject exists at all. Both are computed here, from the migration's own text, and both are in the report per finding (`controlClass`, `subjectNeverCreatedInChain`).

The most useful thing found is not a new exposure. It is that the repository's newest migrations — DB-013's 20260926150000, DB-016's 20260926200000 and WFC-004's 20260927100000 — each carry an inert post-condition assertion, and that the two most recent RLS-block families in the chain are the ones with the largest version gaps (five days, and seven months).

defectsFoundInThisDetector.why: DB-014 shipped two defects in its own new instrument the same day it found the staff_performance_metrics bug. These are the equivalents here, found by running the thing rather than reading it. Each is now pinned by a fixture, and each is recorded because the reusable part is the failure mode, not the fix.

defects.what: The whole condition's polarity was inferred from the presence of a `not exists` ANYWHERE in it, so a CONJUNCTION was inverted.
defects.symptom: `if to_regclass('public.organizations') is not null and not exists (select 1 from pg_constraint ...) then` was reported never-executed. Both conjuncts are true, so the block RUNS. Four `pg_constraint` guards and five more were wrong in the same direction.
defects.direction: false positive, on files whose names are security migrations
defects.cause: One boolean for a boolean expression, and the `is null` operator sits AFTER its subject so a test of the text before the source read it as `is not null`.
defects.fix: Per-conjunct polarity read from the whole conjunct span, with `is not null` checked before `not`/`is null`; and a condition whose conjuncts do not pair one-to-one with modelled sources is `unanalysed` rather than decided.

defects.what: Only the `then` arm was measured, so an INVERTED guard (`if X is null then null; else <control> end if`) reported the `null;` as the never-executed control.
defects.symptom: Three staffing RLS policies in 20260414140000_fix_security_linter_views_and_rls.sql — `staffing_overview_cache`, `staffing_api_telemetry`, `staffing_alert_events`, each `alter table ... enable row level security` plus a venue-scoped select policy — were reported as never-created controls. They are created. The tables exist and the `else` arm runs.
defects.direction: false positive, and the most seductive kind: the finding looked exactly like DB015-K1
defects.cause: The control was assumed to be in the `then` arm, and the `then` span ran to `end if`, so it swallowed the `else` arm and both arms looked occupied.
defects.fix: The `else` arm is extracted, the `then` span ends at `else`, and the arm carrying the control decides the verdict's direction. A control in both arms is `unanalysed`; no control in either arm is not a finding.

defects.what: A drop-policy block aimed at a policy that NO migration creates was reported at HIGH severity.
defects.symptom: `20260414120000:521` was HIGH, on the grounds that the permissive `System can insert delivery logs` survives. The chain creates no policy by that name, and notification_delivery_log's own creating migration installs two differently-named policies, so nothing survives.
defects.direction: false positive at the highest severity this check can emit
defects.cause: The drop target was matched as the next bare word after `drop policy if exists`, which for a QUOTED name with spaces is `on`. The name harvest read a policy named `on`, which the chain does create, and the severity rule believed it.
defects.fix: Identifier read by exact offset from the raw text with quote handling, and a policy-removal block is only HIGH when the chain actually creates a policy of that name.
fixtures: the severityReason field on every DB015-K7 finding

defects.what: A `\s+` at the end of a keyword pattern ate the mask's blanks and handed the next bare word to the name reader.
defects.symptom: The same `on` capture as SELF-3, from a second site.
defects.cause: In a mask, a blanked-out string literal is indistinguishable from whitespace, so a trailing `\s*` consumes it.
defects.fix: No trailing whitespace class in any keyword pattern; the value is read from the raw text by offset.

defects.what: The mask blanks every dollar-quoted span, so scanning a DO block or a function body through the whole-file mask found NOTHING, and no guard site was discovered in the entire chain.
defects.direction: the worst kind: a clean report from a broken instrument
defects.cause: A DO body is a dollar-quoted span, so to the file the whole body is one literal.
defects.fix: Every nested region is re-scanned in its own right. The anti-vacuity guard would also have caught this: `assertAnchorsSeen` refuses a clean report when the two confirmed instances are not found, so this could not have shipped as a clean chain.

notDefectsButWorthNaming: A `if to_regclass(X) is null then return; end if; <rest>` guard has a LARGER blast radius than a single-statement guard — it skips everything after the `end if` — but reports as `guard-true` when the author got it right. A detector that only counts never-executed statements understates it; `statementsSkipped` is reported per finding for that reason.

Within one migration, a guard ABOVE a `create table` is a real instance of this defect that needs no cross-file reasoning at all. `20250130000001_tour_teams.sql:81` is the only one in the chain, and it is a good example precisely because it is self-inflicted.

limits: A chain replay cannot tell you what a TARGET contains. Every claim here is a claim about the ordered source. DB-002 found out-of-band Management API application, so a target may differ in either direction, and DB-013's migration ships anyway for exactly this reason.
Guards inside FUNCTION bodies are out of scope: they evaluate at call time against a live catalog, not at a version position.
